item.title: Make polluters pay: From Mannar to the world, communities demand
item.description:
At Keeri Beach in Mannar, in Sri Lanka’s far north, about 250 people stood together under the scorching sun in blue gowns, lining the water’s edge with hands joined and arms raised toward the sea.
Who is responsible for climate change? Who will pay for the loss and damage? People from every walk of life kept asking as they took part in an installation by Indian artist Dr Subodh Kerkar for Greenpeace South Asia in the second week of October, ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
A fish processor in Senegal described her family home shrinking from more than 20 rooms to 6, a fisherman in Mannar reported his catch falling from 300kg to 30kg, a campaigner from Papua New Guinea spoke of islands lost to the sea, a cab drivers’ association leader in Hyderabad highlighted drivers enduring hours of extreme heat without shade, and a Bangladeshi participant described hydration points set up in markets for vendors and rickshaw pullers.
Their homes and workplaces are thousands of kilometers apart, but the complaint was the same: those who did the least to cause the climate crisis are living with its effects every day, and those who caused the loss and damage must pay for it.
For Mama Fatou Samba, a fish processor and community leader from Senegal, the sea’s advance is measured in meters and in relatives.
“Forty years ago, we had to swim more than 100 meters to reach the sea. Now, the sea has advanced by more than 100 meters.”
In her area, the coastline reportedly retreats 2 to 3 meters a year, and the water has reached the ground where her house stands.
The family home once had more than 20 rooms; now, only 6 remain as the sea advances, relatives are forced to leave, and a household that had lived together breaks up.
Mama Fatou Samba called that breakdown one of climate change’s most painful consequences, sometimes worse than the financial loss.
Fishing and farming can no longer support a family, she said, and thousands of young people take risky routes to reach Spain and Italy, many from her area.
“They are climate refugees.”
Vinzealhar Ainjo Nen, a participant from Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea, said a culture tied to land and sea by ancestors is now under strain from rising waters, erratic weather, food insecurity and floods.
A participant from Papua New Guinea wearing her traditional dress attended at Mannar. Photo: Ali Asif Shawon/Dhaka Tribune
“For generations, my people have lived with the land and the nature around us, but that has changed. Severe weather events, forest fires, and water scarcity are adversely affecting my community. It is not our actions that cause this, but the choices of those who do not recognize or care about the hardship we face. I came to Mannar because our voices must be heard, and listened to,” she said.
Mannar gave her something else.
“I’m not alone,” she said, describing how people tied to the land can feel stuck “in a bubble.”
Restituto del Rosario, a fisherman from the Philippines, speaking through a translator, delivered a short, grave message: it may already be too late, and the world could lose its fish and the food that comes with them.
“Because our livelihood depends on fishing, extreme heat is hitting us hard. We did not create this crisis, but we live with its cost. Standing here in Mannar with communities from across the world, our message is simple: the fossil fuel companies responsible for this must pay,” he said.
Qunson Marynathan, an independent climate researcher based in Mannar, said that after nearly 30 years at sea, his catch used to be 300 to 400kg, but now it is 30 to 40kg.
Qunson compared that day’s temperature of about 31 degrees Celsius with a 30-year October average of around 30 degrees, a rise of roughly 0.8 degrees.
These are his own readings, not an official record, but his larger point does not depend on them: Mannar sits among very shallow seas, and shallow water heats easily.
His grievance was with how outsiders study the place.
“What goes missing in the eyes of many reporters or researchers is the people,” he said.
Mannar hosts many migratory bird species and has been inhabited for some 2,000 years, appearing on Ptolemy’s maps.
“When you take us, the people, out of the equation, it’s not there. Come talk to me first,” he said.
He described heat as something the body feels.
“Go to the streets under the sun on a very heavy day. You try to negotiate with somebody who’s selling something, and they start shouting at you. This is not the culture of the people. This is also being caused by climate change.”
His children had been unwell for days.
“I didn’t heat up the sun. I didn’t heat up the ocean,” he said.
Dr S Wijeyamohan of the University of Vavuniya’s Department of Bio-Science said the ocean absorbs heat and carbon dioxide, stabilizing the climate, but that capacity is not unlimited.
A Bangladeshi participant, Kouser Alam, described a response already underway on the streets.
With Greenpeace’s help, they set up hydration points in major markets over the past year, serving vendors, rickshaw pullers and construction workers.
“We are not just raising our voice against these issues. We are trying to solve the issue also,” Kouser said.
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
Shaik Salahuddin, a cab drivers’ association leader from Hyderabad, said drivers and delivery workers move between air-conditioned cars and punishing outdoor heat all day, a strain on body and mind.
He said platform companies advertise concern for gig workers, “but that is only from PR.”
At Hyderabad’s international airport, drivers wait 4 to 5 hours in a car park with 4,000 to 5,000 vehicles, no trees and little shade.
Platforms pay ₹10 extra when it rains, he said, but nothing when the heat turns dangerous.
“The platform companies are also not accountable and transparent,” he said.
Guidelines exist, but “only on paper, not in real realities.”
Meenakshi, a street vegetable seller from India, described a squeeze from both sides. Vendors buy extra water to sprinkle on produce and wet sacks to cover it. Costs rise while earnings fall because fewer customers want to shop in the heat.
Amanullah Porag, a youth climate activist from Bangladesh, said: “Where I live, rising water is not a prediction — it is already taking land, homes and livelihoods. Families are being pushed to move, again and again. This is not a natural disaster; it is the result of decisions made far away from us, by companies that have profited while we lose everything. We came to Mannar to stand in solidarity with global south communities as accountability cannot wait any longer.”
Why in Mannar? When asked, Binu Jacob, executive director of Greenpeace South Asia, said: “Mannar is unique in many ways, with its rich biodiversity, its connection to the ocean and communities that have depended on the sea for centuries. But what is happening here is not just a story about Mannar. It reflects the experiences of fishing and farming communities across South Asia and around the world.”
“Those who contribute least to climate change are often paying a heavy price for the lifestyles and economic activities of others. Climate accountability means asking why these communities must bear the consequences while industries and countries continue to profit from carbon-emitting activities and pollute the environment,” he said.
“We have only one planet. Communities worldwide are already raising these concerns, and we are joining their efforts to share their experiences with a wider audience. Our aim is to help people see the connections between climate change, livelihoods and responsibility,” said Binu, who joined Mannar with a team of volunteers by cycling more than 300 kilometers from Colombo.
Dr Subodh Kerkar, a doctor who became an ocean artist, called the installation “a protest and a prayer.”
Artist Dr Subodh Kerkar talking about his works at Mannar. Photo: Ali Asif Shawon/Dhaka Tribune
“Art is not a slogan. Art is a whisper. Art has to be subtle. We don't have to shout, ‘I love the ocean’ or ‘I want to protect the ocean.’ Standing together in the water and raising our hands is itself an act of protection, an act of connection and an act of love for the ocean,” he said about his artwork at Mannar.
“The life of a fisherman and the life of the ocean cannot be separated. The ocean is very much a part of a fisherman's life, and that inseparability is what I try to express through my work,” he said.
When asked why they chose Mannar, Subodh said: “Mannar is only an example, a metaphor. What we have done here is not just for Mannar; it is for the globe. These things are happening worldwide, not just in Mannar. The sea is rising, the heat is rising, and the people are also rising.”
The demand doesn't stop at the coast; as Bal Krishna Sah, senior correspondent at The Himalayan Times, pointed out, Nepal has been living through this.
“What Nepal has been experiencing since August 26 is evidence enough of the suffering that climate change can inflict on people who had little say in causing it, and who often do not know what is driving such a devastating disaster. If incidents like these do not make people change their ways, what will?”
Asked about the recent Nepal disaster, Subodh said investigations continue, but the people who died “had no role to play in that chunk of ice falling down.”
Climate change harms people with the least say and the least protection most, whether that’s a family in Senegal losing its home to the sea, fishermen in Mannar hauling in a tenth of their old catch, or outdoor workers in Hyderabad and Dhaka enduring dangerous heat.
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
Their demands are consistent: pair community observations with scientific evidence so polluters can be held accountable; fund adaptation, not just mitigation; provide shade, water, rest areas and fair pay for outdoor workers; and consult the people affected.
The speakers were careful not to overclaim. Local problems rarely have a single cause, and showing harm is not the same as proving who is to blame, so credible climate justice needs both the evidence and the accountability.
Asked what message he would leave, Subodh returned to the oldest argument.
“We have not inherited the earth from our parents or grandparents. We have borrowed it from our children. We need to give our earth back to the children in a good state. They deserve a better earth.”

item.title: More than 1,000 arrested daily as Bangladesh prisons exceed capacity
item.description:
A documentary published this week on the Facebook page of the Bangladesh Department of Prisons showcased well-furnished facilities, quality food, gymnasiums and skills development programmes for inmates. However, current and former inmates say the reality inside prisons is markedly different, as authorities struggle to manage a prison population more than double the system's capacity.
Law enforcement agencies have been arresting more than 1,000 people daily through regular and special operations aimed at curbing crime. Weapons, ammunition, drugs and locally made firearms are also being recovered during these drives.
In an operation by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), 510 people were arrested and 48 cases filed in the capital over the past 24 hours. Despite the large number of arrests, however, crimes including murder, mugging, extortion, drug-related offences and juvenile gang activities remain difficult to control, raising concerns about the country's law and order situation.
Meanwhile, a study published in the United Kingdom has found that Bangladesh has the highest prison overcrowding rate relative to capacity among South Asian countries. For every 100 places available in the country's prisons, there are 226 inmates.
Crime analysts say arrests are only the first step towards controlling crime, arguing that proper investigations and swift justice are not being ensured. They also say criminals continue to flout the law because law enforcement agencies are failing to take sufficiently stringent measures to prevent crime.
According to DMP figures, 5,005 people were arrested on various allegations in the capital over 11 days, from October 1 to October 11. During the same period, 580 cases were filed for various offences, with the number of arrests averaging 455 a day.
Data from the Police Headquarters show that 53,518 people were arrested during special police operations between May 1 and August 26, 2026. Including approximately 150,000 arrests in other cases and operations, the total stood at 195,146, averaging around 1,650 arrests a day.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday afternoon, Additional Inspector General of Police at the Police Headquarters Md Sayedur Rahman said: “Arrest is only a process of bringing a criminal under the law. Crime cannot be controlled through arrests alone. Prevention is another measure. If there is a risk of deterioration in the law and order situation somewhere, the police take preventive action.
“To reduce crime, social resistance must also be built alongside the efforts of law enforcement agencies. If someone repeatedly commits the same offence, they must be brought under exemplary punishment.”
Sri Lanka is close to Bangladesh in terms of prison overcrowding, while India and Pakistan are in comparatively better positions.
World Prison Brief (WPB), an online database maintained by the Institute for Crime and Justice Policy Research at Birkbeck, University of London, publishes statistics on prison populations worldwide. Its data on Bangladesh are based on information from the Department of Prisons.
According to WPB, Bangladesh's prisons have an official capacity of 45,186 inmates. In September this year, the prison population stood at 102,180, meaning the facilities were operating at 226.1% of their intended capacity. The country has 59 prisoners for every 100,000 people.
Data from the Department of Prisons indicate that the inmate population has increased further. As of October 14, the number of inmates stood at 130,128 against an official capacity of 45,186.
Among other South Asian countries, prison populations stand at 216% of capacity in Sri Lanka, 163% in Pakistan, 144% in Nepal, 113% in India and 112% in Myanmar.
Globally, the Republic of the Congo has the highest prison occupancy rate, at 617% of capacity. Nauru has the lowest, with its prisons holding inmates equivalent to just 14% of their intended capacity.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday afternoon, Additional Inspector General of Prisons Md Jahangir Kabir said: “The 75 prisons in the country have a total capacity of 45,186 inmates. Currently, there are more than 100,000 prisoners. We struggle to manage the pressure caused by the excess number of inmates. Our workload increases, and we also have to perform additional duties.”
He added: “If a family has five members and another five guests arrive, it creates pressure on that family. We are facing the same kind of pressure.”
According to the Department of Prisons website, Bangladesh's prison system dates back to 1788, when a criminal ward was established in Dhaka. Prisons were subsequently built in Dhaka, Rajshahi, Jessore and Comilla in 1836. The Dhaka and Rajshahi prisons were declared central prisons in 1929.
The country now has 75 prisons, including 15 central prisons and 60 district prisons.
According to WPB data, 66.9% of inmates in Bangladesh's prisons are pretrial detainees. This means approximately two-thirds of those behind bars have yet to be sentenced.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday evening, Assistant Inspector General of Prisons (Development) Muhammad Enayet Ullah said: “As of October 14, the total number of inmates stood at 130,128. More than 75,000 of them are awaiting trial. The number of prisoners awaiting trial is increasing the pressure on prisons.”
Although Bangladesh's prisons hold nearly three times their official capacity according to the latest Department of Prisons figures, medical services remain inadequate. Fifty-four prisons have no ambulances, while only two permanent doctors are available against 151 sanctioned positions.
The longstanding medical crisis in the country's prisons means inmates sometimes die on their way to hospitals when they require emergency treatment. Questions have also been raised about the quality of food served to prisoners, while complaints about prolonged delays in securing bail have persisted for years.
A recently released former inmate told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding in prisons had increased significantly.
“There is no room anywhere, from the toilets to the sleeping areas. We have to live crammed together in congested conditions. It is almost as if one person's nose touches another person's nose. The food is not particularly good either. There are cockroaches, mosquitoes and flies. The excessive number of people creates a terrible stench. We have to sleep packed tightly together on the floor,” he said.
He added: “The most alarming thing is that when someone falls ill, a doctor is not available. There are also no ambulances to take them to hospital. I have seen people suffer strokes and die before my eyes, and there is nothing we can do.”
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday, senior Supreme Court lawyer Mohammed Saeed Ahmed Raza said: “Recently, we have seen arrests in political cases, particularly arrests followed by shown arrests. More than 1,500 people are being arrested daily. However, prisons do not have enough space to accommodate them.
“This violates the human rights of accused persons, while the excessive pressure on inmates is making the judicial system completely fragile. The state must ensure that no one remains imprisoned without committing a crime.”
According to WPB and a 2024 study, mental health conditions in prisons across Southeast Asia are a serious and neglected concern. Overcrowding and a severe shortage of mental health services have contributed to the prevalence of mental disorders among prisoners in the region, with estimates ranging from 40% to 100%.
Prison sources say each prison has a designated post for a psychiatrist, but none has a specialist in the position. Inmates in almost all prisons are living in inhumane conditions and suffering from mental and physical health problems without receiving adequate treatment.
Prisoners with health conditions require regular counselling and specialised treatment. There are also no doctors specifically assigned to care for inmates with disabilities.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Additional Inspector General of Prisons Md Jahangir Kabir said: “There are no mental health specialists in prisons. If an inmate requires psychiatric treatment, we send them to the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital. We provide medical services with assistance from district civil surgeons. We also face a shortage of ambulances.”
He said the problems had been communicated to the Ministry of Health and the relevant government departments.
Asked why crime remains difficult to control despite the large number of arrests, Dhaka University teacher and crime expert Dr Md Tawohidul Haque told Dhaka Tribune that shortcomings in law enforcement, political and social influence, and structural weaknesses were among the main reasons.
He said some accused people exploit legal loopholes and prolonged judicial proceedings to secure their release before becoming involved in crime again.
The crime expert said arrests alone could not control crime, stressing the need for impartial investigations and swift justice.

item.title: Bangladesh unaware of execution of two citizens in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Bangladesh was unaware of the execution of two of its citizens in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, over alleged “immoral” acts at a mosque, learning of the matter only through media reports.
The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah subsequently wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday, seeking details of the executions, according to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka and the consulate.
A consular source said on Friday afternoon that Saudi authorities had not formally notified Bangladesh before carrying out the executions. The consulate learned of the matter through media reports and then sought an official explanation from the Saudi foreign ministry.
The Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the country's Interior Ministry, confirmed the executions on Wednesday. The two Bangladeshis were identified as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar.
Middle East-based news outlet Gulf News reported that Saudi security forces had arrested the two over allegations of engaging in immoral and indecent acts at a mosque in Makkah.
According to the report, they were charged following an initial investigation and referred to court. The court sentenced them to death under ta'zir, a category of discretionary punishment under Sharia law. The judge reportedly considered the violation of the mosque's sanctity and the circumstances of the alleged offence when delivering the verdict.
Higher judicial authorities later upheld the verdict, making it final, before a royal order was issued for the executions.
In a statement, the Saudi Interior Ministry reaffirmed the government's commitment to protecting the sanctity of the holy mosques, upholding justice and enforcing Sharia law against those who violate religious sanctity. It also warned that similar offences at holy sites would attract severe punishment.
Private sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial had been underway at a court in Jeddah for several months. Two prominent Bangladeshi citizens reportedly assisted in the proceedings as interpreters.
Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Under Article 36, if a foreign national is arrested, the detaining country must inform the person's consulate without delay if the detainee requests it and facilitate consular communication and assistance.
It remains unclear whether the two Bangladeshis had requested that the Bangladeshi consulate be notified.
Several officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the executions were unlikely to have taken place immediately after the arrests, given the judicial process involved. They also questioned why no one acting on behalf of the two had contacted the Bangladeshi mission during their detention.
No information has yet emerged about the nature or duration of the two Bangladeshis' stay in Saudi Arabia, or whether they received legal assistance or had an opportunity to appeal during the proceedings.

item.title: Shyamsiddhir Math - a monument that pierces the sky
item.description:
A couple of weeks ago, on a crisp morning, I found myself cruising down the beautiful Dhaka-Mawa Highway. I was heading towards Sreenagar in Munshiganj. All along the route, the fluffy white feathers of catkin bushes danced between the asphalt and the parallel rail tracks—a breathtaking visual testimony to the arrival of autumn.
While my final destination for the day was Arial Beel, a vast wetland, I decided to take a spontaneous detour at Shyamsiddhi, a Union under Sreenagar. There lays a hidden gem, tucked away in the tranquility of rural life – Shyamsiddhir Math. This math is a two-century-old architectural marvel that pierces the sky.
A closer view of the Shyamsiddhir Math, looking upward through the surrounding lush greenery and coconut palm fronds. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
I am no stranger to math monuments in Bangladesh, having explored many across different regions, including the famous Sonarang Twin Math in the neighboring Tongibari Upazila. Yet, nothing quite prepares you for the sheer scale of Shyamsiddhir Math. Standing at an imposing height estimated anything between 220 to 240 feet, it easily dwarfs the others.
The structure features complex brick ornamentation at its octagonal base and transitions into a sharply tapered conical spire. Though weathered over time, it remains an architectural marvel and a significant tourist attraction in the Munshiganj region. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Built in the early 19th century by a wealthy merchant named Shambunath Majumdar to honor his deceased father, historical records note it as the tallest math in Bangladesh and one of the highest in the entire Indian subcontinent. The slight variation in its exact recorded height depends on whether you include the ancient, massive iron trident that still proudly crowns the apex of its spire.
For travel writers, spelling math in English is always a bit of a riddle, given its myriad South Asian variants like matha, moth, or mutt. Linguistic nuances aside, the very concept of math carries diverse connotations. While its Sanskrit root refers to a monastery or a place of learning for monks, the word has evolved in our part of the world. Today, it can mean a Hindu monastery, an ashram, or—most commonly—a distinctive, cone-shaped commemorative monument.
The lower left corner features a modern white sign written in Bengali script. It reads: Shri Shri Sarbojonin Shiba Math, Shyamsiddhi, Location: Adjacent to Shyamsiddhi Union Parishad, Srinagar, Munshiganj, Built in 1836. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
My own travels confirm that across rural Bangladesh and near old Zamindari (landlord) estates, these tall, slender, sharply pointed structures function primarily as cremation monuments (Chita Mandir). Built over the cremation sites of prominent landlords, saints, or family elders, they serve as soaring, brick-and-mortar tributes to the deceased.
The renovated ground-level entrance door facade to the main inner sanctum at the base of the math. Over the years, the lower base section was modernized with these white tiles and printed pictures of Lord Shiva, complete with the prominent red arch trim over the main entrance. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Approaching the site through a neighborhood dotted with traditional tin and wooden stilt houses, the dense greenery surrounding the monument caught my eye first. Then there was that unforgettable sight and sound of pandemonium of parakeets hovering overhead before diving back into the structure.
Over the years, structural decay has created hundreds of tiny crevices and holes near the top tier. Nature has beautifully reclaimed this decay, organically transforming the ancient monument into a lively bird sanctuary. Framed by thriving coconut, mango, and guava trees, the upper sections of the tapered monument also host opportunistic parasitic vegetation. Small wild fig and banyan saplings stubbornly take root directly out of the high brick fissures.
The hollow alcoves within the tower make it a famous sanctuary for hundreds of parakeets. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Architecturally, Shyamsiddhir Math is a masterclass in 19th-century artisanship. It is a robust, octagonal brick structure built using traditional chun-surki — a highly durable heritage mortar made of slaked lime and powdered burnt clay. Its structural blueprint features a base measuring 21 feet in both length and width (though some archaeological records classify the external bounding box as a six-meter square) with foundational walls stretching roughly a meter deep.
These numerous deep square recesses scattered across the octagonal brick walls are the exact openings where hundreds of wild parakeets and parrots build their nests, making the structure a prominent local ecological attraction. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
The monument rises in three distinct vertical stages: at the base – a lower square section serving as the primary sanctum, featuring a prominent entrance adorned with a pointed arch on its southern façade; in mid-section – heavy brickwork begins to taper inward; and finally an internal chamber that seamlessly transitions into a narrowing spire stretches up to its pinnacle.
The writer standing in front of a beautifully crafted, elevated wooden house just opposite to the Shyamsiddhir Math. Built in a traditional regional architectural style, this house features white wall panels, dark wood frames, and ornate geometric latticework along the roofline. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Today, these heavily perforated upper exterior walls are a thriving ecological haven. Inhabited by hundreds of native birds—predominantly parakeets and crested mynas—the ancient brickwork stays vibrantly alive with their chirping.
This mid-angle perspective captures the sweeping, upward taper of the Shyamsiddhir Math, emphasizing its immense scale against the rural skyline. If one looks closely at the upper edges and crevices, s/he can see small dark silhouettes of birds perched along the sides, highlighting its lively status as a natural aviary. Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
Long after I left the premises and advanced toward the sweeping waters of Arial Beel, I could still see the math's spire slicing through the horizon from miles away. It stands like a historic lighthouse over the green plains of Munshiganj—a poetic reminder of past craftsmanship, familial love, and the wild resilience of nature.

item.title: Plan to cap lawyers’ entry age at 35 draws mixed reactions
item.description:
A proposal to set 35 as the maximum age for enrolment as a lawyer in Bangladesh has sparked mixed reactions in the legal community, with some backing the move to improve professional standards and others warning that it could unfairly exclude aspiring lawyers who pursue the profession later in life.
Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman announced the initiative at an event at the Supreme Court on October 13, saying the government was working to bar people aged over 35 from entering the legal profession.
He also said the Bar Council’s Legal Education Committee had passed a resolution on the matter. Dhaka Tribune has obtained a copy of the resolution dated August 19, signed by Attorney General Barrister Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal and Bar Council Secretary Mohammad Kamal Hossain Sikdar.
The document contains an extract from the minutes of the Bar Council meeting held on August 19, 2026, under agenda item six, concerning recommendations made by the Legal Education Committee.
According to the resolution, the committee recommended setting a reasonable upper age limit for enrolment as a lawyer in light of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No 253 of 2014 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court.
The committee argued that an upper age limit would help enhance the dignity and competence of the legal profession, encourage long-term professional engagement and make the profession more dynamic.
At a meeting on August 6, 2026, the committee proposed setting the maximum age at 35 and placed the recommendation before the Bar Council. Following detailed discussions, all members present agreed to the proposal, which was adopted unanimously. The resolution states that the new limit will take effect on January 1, 2030.
The decision has drawn criticism from some members of the legal community, while others have expressed qualified support. Critics argue that an age limit could disadvantage those whose education has been delayed by academic session backlogs or who turn to law after pursuing other careers. Some have also pointed out that countries such as England do not impose an upper age limit on entry into the profession.
Imam Hossain, an apprentice lawyer at a subordinate court in Dhaka, told Dhaka Tribune that he was disappointed by the decision.
“Due to session backlogs, many students in Bangladesh are already older by the time they complete their studies. If someone fails to secure a government job within the prescribed age limit and then wants to enter the legal profession, what is the harm in that? No country in the world imposes an age limit for entering this profession,” he said.
“We want the decision to be reversed. Otherwise, we will call for a movement,” he added. Attorney General Barrister Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal told Dhaka Tribune that the initiative aimed to improve professionalism, competence and the standing of the legal profession while encouraging long-term career engagement.
Under Article 27(1) of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972, applicants must be at least 21 years old and meet the prescribed educational and examination requirements to enrol as lawyers. The existing provision does not specify a maximum age.
If implemented, the proposed limit would mark a significant change in the rules governing entry into the legal profession.
Barrister Sanjid Siddiqui, an executive committee member of the Supreme Court Bar Association, described the proposal as timely, citing the growing number of lawyers and the challenges of providing them with adequate facilities.
He said the Supreme Court had around 18,000 lawyers, while the Dhaka Bar Association had approximately 40,000. The total number of lawyers nationwide was estimated at around 80,000.
Providing adequate training, suitable working spaces at bar associations, research facilities and library services had become increasingly difficult amid the growing number of practitioners, he said.
“Priority should be given to the best students who have aspired to become lawyers from the beginning and want to build their careers in this profession, rather than treating it as a second or alternative career,” Siddiqui said.
He reiterated that the rapid increase in the number of lawyers made the proposed age limit timely. However, he acknowledged that countries such as England did not impose an upper age limit on entry into the profession.
“Law is an independent profession, so imposing an age limit is not entirely appropriate. However, given the growing number of lawyers, it is also essential to ensure adequate training and other necessary facilities,” he added.
Supreme Court lawyer Monjila Jhuma said improving the quality of the legal profession required more than an age restriction.
She called for a robust merit-based selection process, effective mandatory practical training, adequate training opportunities for junior lawyers and continuous assessments of professional competence.
Jhuma said the views of lawyers, the Bar Council, legal academics and other stakeholders in the justice system should be considered before an upper age limit was introduced.
She said the rules governing entry into the profession should encourage talented young people while ensuring fairness for those who wished to become lawyers later in life because of their educational backgrounds, previous experience or other practical circumstances.
“However, there must be no compromise on professional standards, ethics and competence,” she said.
Jhuma added that protecting the dignity of the legal profession required quality legal education, effective training, professional accountability and strict enforcement of ethical standards, alongside merit-based selection.
A comprehensive policy addressing these issues, she said, would improve the quality of legal practice and strengthen access to justice.

item.title: Coast Guard deploys 3,500 personnel for Durga Puja security
item.description:
The Bangladesh Coast Guard has deployed around 3,500 personnel across its areas of responsibility to ensure security during Sharadiya Durga Puja, with special arrangements in place at 615 temples and puja mandaps.
Coast Guard Director General Rear Admiral Md Moinul Hasan disclosed the information during a visit to Mirpur Central Temple yesterday morning to inspect security arrangements ahead of the festival.
He said the force was working to maintain law and order and protect the lives and property of the public during the celebrations.
Of the 615 temples and puja mandaps under the Coast Guard's security coverage, 63 are in the East Zone, 144 in the West Zone, 371 in the South Zone and 37 in the Dhaka Zone, he said.
The Coast Guard has also intensified intelligence surveillance and is working in coordination with other law enforcement agencies to ensure that members of the Hindu community can celebrate Durga Puja peacefully and safely.
To prevent accidents on waterways during the festival, the force has continued public awareness campaigns and round-the-clock patrols. Special diving teams will remain on standby at idol immersion sites to respond to potential accidents.
The director general urged the public to contact the Coast Guard's emergency hotline, 16111, for assistance in the event of any untoward incident.
He said the Coast Guard would continue its public safety initiatives to maintain security during religious festivals and protect people and property.

item.title: ASK calls for impartial probe, justice over journalist’s killing
item.description:
Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) has called for an impartial investigation and justice for those responsible over the shooting death of journalist Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir in Netrokona’s Durgapur.
The human rights organisation also urged the authorities to take effective measures to prevent attacks, threats and killings targeting journalists.
ASK made the demands in a statement issued on Friday.
According to media reports cited in the statement, Alif Fakir was shot at Uttarail Bazar on the Shyamganj-Birishiri Road of Durgapur on the night of October 15.
He worked as the Netrokona correspondent for private IPTV channel Ruposhi Bangla. He had previously been attacked in November 2025. ASK said the failure to ensure his safety after the earlier attack, followed by his killing, was deeply concerning.
The organisation said the shooting death of a journalist was not only an attack on an individual’s life but also sent a dangerous message for press freedom, freedom of expression and the public’s right to know.
Failure to investigate and prosecute violence and killings targeting journalists would create an atmosphere of fear, narrowing the space for independent reporting on issues of public interest and undermining democratic accountability and the rule of law, it said.
Citing Articles 32 and 39 of the Constitution, ASK said the rights to life and freedom of expression and the press are protected under these provisions. Similarly, Articles 6 and 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) recognise the rights to life and freedom of expression.
Ensuring journalists’ safety and conducting effective investigations and prosecutions into violence against them are the state’s responsibilities, it said.
On Alif Fakir’s killing and the need for justice, ASK Executive Director Tahmina Rahman said there should be no negligence, influence or bias in the investigation.
“Everyone involved in the killing must be identified and brought to justice,” she said, calling for justice through an impartial and effective investigation.
ASK also urged the authorities to create an environment where journalists can perform their professional duties without threats or fear.
“Protecting independent journalism is not merely a matter of professional interest; it is a prerequisite for democracy, human rights and an accountable state,” the organisation said.

item.title: Home minister: BNP government ensures biggest Puja celebrations this year
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Friday said this year, under the BNP government, has witnessed the highest number of Durga Puja mandaps, the highest allocation of funds, the longest holidays and the biggest celebrations.
“The highest number of puja mandaps have been set up this time, the highest allocation has been made, the longest holidays have been given, and the celebrations are at their peak. The highest number of votes was also recorded this time, and it will happen again,” he said, while speaking as the chief guest during a visit to a Durga Puja mandap at Banani field in the capital on Friday night.
He stressed the importance of ensuring religious freedom, constitutional rights and security for people of all faiths in Bangladesh, saying there should be no discrimination on religious grounds.
The Constitution guarantees every citizen the right to practise religious rituals freely, worship according to their faith and establish places of worship, he said.
Salahuddin said it is unfortunate that the issue of security repeatedly came up during Durga Puja celebrations.
“It makes us feel bad when, during Durga Puja, we repeatedly hear calls to ensure security, celebrate Puja safely and cover everyone with a blanket of security,” he said.
He said people of all religions should be able to celebrate their respective festivals without hindrance, adding that a situation in which people had to seek security to observe religious festivals was regrettable for the country.
“It is very unfortunate for our national life that this issue continues to arise. This should never happen,” he said.
The minister said he preferred the term “religious harmony” to “communal harmony”, which he said was often used when discussing relations among people of different faiths.
He said people had not come together as separate communities and that the country's laws did not classify citizens on the basis of religious communities.
“We are all citizens of Bangladesh, and we all have equal rights,” he said.
The minister said people of all religions had equal rights as citizens and that such rights were recognised in countries around the world, regardless of which religion formed the majority.
He said people of the Hindu community should be regarded as followers of their religion, rather than as a separate community.
“Some people may regard you as a community, and many have used you in the past for political gain. We will not go into that issue,” he said.
“But as citizens of Bangladesh and as free citizens, you will judge for yourselves during which democratic period your democratic and constitutional rights remain protected. The decision is yours. You do not need to be anyone's vote bank. You are accountable to your own conscience,” he said.
The minister expressed hope that people would be able to celebrate Durga Puja and all other religious festivals freely, peacefully and joyfully this year, next year and in the years to come.
Earlier, Inspector General of Police Ali Hossain Fakir, Dhaka Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mosleh Uddin Ahmed, the British high commissioner, and the ambassadors of Canada, Norway, Switzerland and Nepal addressed the program.

item.title: Jamaat dissolves Comilla city unit in aftermath of after Wednesday clash
item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami has dissolved its Comilla city unit following a clash at its city office on Wednesday and formed a two-member committee to investigate the incident.
The party’s central executive council took the decisions at an emergency meeting at its central office in the capital on Thursday evening, chaired by Jamaat Ameer and Leader of the Opposition Dr Shafiqur Rahman, according to a press release issued on Friday.
The probe committee comprises Jamaat Nayeb-e-Ameer ATM Azharul Islam, MP, and Assistant Secretary General Maulana Muhammad Shahjahan.
The committee has been asked to submit its investigation report to the party chief within a week. The central executive council will decide on further action after reviewing the findings.
Under the decisions, both the organizational structure and leadership of the Comilla city unit have been dissolved in accordance with the party constitution.
The unit will now operate under the supervision of the central organization, with Assistant Secretary General Maulana Abdul Halim assigned to oversee its activities on behalf of the centre.
The Wednesday clash reportedly broke out among rival factions at the Comilla city unit office amid disagreements over the formation of a new city committee and the selection of its next Ameer.
The incident occurred around 7pm, and the vehicle of city unit Secretary Mahabubur Rahman was vandalized.
The emergency meeting was convened to review the Wednesday incident at the Jamaat office in Comilla and the situation arising from it.

item.title: BRAC University hosts women’s cricket tournament to mark 25th anniversary
item.description:
BRAC University hosted the Ayesha Abed T-10 Inter-University Women’s Cricket Tournament to mark its 25th anniversary, bringing together teams from 12 universities in a two-day competition that concluded on Thursday.
Daffodil International University defeated Uttara University by 121 runs in the final to win the tournament.
State Minister for Youth and Sports Aminul Islam inaugurated the tournament, emphasizing the importance of creating opportunities for students to pursue sports professionally alongside their studies.
Photo: Courtesy
He also highlighted the need to ensure year-round sporting opportunities for students and expressed interest in collaboration with private universities to promote sports.
BRAC University Pro-Vice-Chancellor Professor Arshad Mahmud Chowdhury said students need opportunities to maintain their physical and mental well-being while developing diverse skills beyond the classroom.
The university’s Treasurer, Ariful Islam, said BRAC University was working to develop its sports infrastructure.
Photo: Courtesy
The tournament was organized in honour of Ayesha Abed, wife of BRAC founder Sir Fazle Hasan Abed and a key organizer within the organization. She worked to empower rural women, expand employment opportunities and organize marginalized communities through awareness-raising and livelihood initiatives.
Following her death, the Ayesha Abed Foundation was established to continue supporting rural women’s self-reliance and economic empowerment.
The tournament also aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 3, which focuses on good health and well-being, and SDG 5, which promotes gender equality.
Twelve institutions participated in the competition: BRAC University, Daffodil International University, Uttara University, North South University, Independent University, Bangladesh, University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh, East West University, Northern University Bangladesh, Bangladesh University of Business and Technology, International University of Business Agriculture and Technology, University of Asia Pacific, and Stamford University Bangladesh.
Photo: Courtesy
Shayla Sumaiya Srishti, a student of Nutrition and Food Engineering at Daffodil International University, scored four centuries in five matches, including 114 runs off 27 balls in the final. She was named Player of the Tournament.
Puja Rani Sarkar, a Law student, was named Best Bowler after taking two hat-tricks during the competition.
Daffodil International University received Tk100,000 as champions, while runners-up Uttara University received Tk50,000.
National women’s cricket team player Juairiya Ferdous Joyita, BRAC University Registrar Dr David Dowland and Head of Student Life Tahsina Rahman presented the trophies.
